summary: Basic SIP security cannot reliably prove who originated a call or message, especially between different domains. This document defines a SIP header field that carries a signature over the caller's identity plus a reference to the credentials needed to check it. It replaces the earlier approach in RFC 4474.

plainLanguage.summary: A Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) request can claim that a call came from a particular person or number, but the claim alone is not proof. This RFC defines a signed Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) that another service can check.

questions: how does sip verify the caller identity
what is the sip identity header
how does stir verify caller id
subtitle: How SIP requests carry a signed assertion of caller identity that another service can verify.

tldr.problem: A SIP request can claim an identity in its From field without giving the recipient a way to verify that claim cryptographically.
tldr.mechanism: An authentication service checks the originator and signs a PASSporT based on request identities and time; a verification service checks the signature using the signer's credential.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8224 replaces RFC 4474, supports telephone numbers and SIP URIs, and leaves credential systems and authorization policy to other specifications. It is updated by RFC 8946.

today: RFC 8224 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4474. It has been updated by RFC 8946.

sections.title: The Caller Identity Problem
sections.content:
A SIP user can supply the From header value, so a recipient cannot trust it as proof of who originated a request. RFC 8224 defines a way to add a signature and a reference to the signer's credential. The identity may be a canonical SIP address-of-record or a telephone number.

The mechanism uses two logical roles. An authentication service authenticates the originator and signs a request; a verification service checks the signature. Either role may be in a user agent or proxy. Whether a valid signature is trusted and what to do with it depend on local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A caller's name in a SIP request can be forged. This RFC lets a service add a signature that another service can verify.

sections.title: The Identity Header and PASSporT
sections.content:
The Identity header carries a signed PASSporT token and an info URI that points to the signer's credential. The older Identity-Info header is deprecated; its information is now represented by header parameters. A request may contain multiple Identity headers.

The PASSporT contains the origin identity, destination identity, and issue time. Its alg value defaults to ES256. A compact form carries only the signature and is recommended to reduce message size; the full form includes the header and payload and is needed for extensions. The info parameter is included so a verifier can obtain the public key credential.
sections.plainLanguage: The header contains a signed token and a place to obtain the public key needed to check it. The token records who sent the request, who it targets, and when it was signed.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying a Request
sections.content:
Before signing, the authentication service checks that it has authority for the claimed identity, authenticates the originator, and ensures that the request has a sufficiently fresh Date header. It then creates a PASSporT and adds an Identity header. The RFC recommends a freshness interval of 60 seconds.

A verifier checks for a supported PASSporT type, derives the origin identity from SIP signaling, obtains the credential, checks the date, and validates the signature. It must not treat the orig claim in a full PASSporT as the caller identity without comparing it with the SIP request.

Failure responses include 428, 436, 437, and 438; a stale date may result in 403. After a 438 response, an authentication service should retry once using the full PASSporT form if it originally sent the compact form. The RFC leaves decisions about accepting or rejecting the request to local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The authentication service checks the request before signing it. The verification service obtains the public key and checks that the signature matches the request.

sections.title: Credentials and Identity Formatting
sections.content:
The RFC does not require a particular credential system. A credential must let the verifier obtain a public key and determine the identity or number range for which the signer is authorized. The verifier must support retrieving the credential through the URI in the info parameter.

Telephone numbers are canonicalized by removing separators and converting to a globally routable form where possible. SIP URIs are normalized by removing parameters, passwords, and ports, then applying case and percent-encoding normalization. Both sides use these forms when constructing and checking the token.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to write a phone number or SIP address in the same standard form before checking the signature. A separate credential system establishes which identities a signing key may represent.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
The signature covers identity information, the request date, the destination, and, when present, certain media fingerprints. These values help prevent an attacker from copying a valid signature into a different request. The mechanism is intended to address impersonation; an attacker can still remove the Identity header, and its absence alone cannot prove that a request is fraudulent.

The signature does not cover the display name, Contact, Call-ID, CSeq, or the whole message body. Assurance also depends on how the signing service authenticates its users and whether the verifier trusts its credential. The full token may reveal a canonicalized telephone number that is not otherwise visible in the request.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid signature can show that a trusted signer approved the claimed identity, but it cannot stop an intermediary from removing the header. The mechanism does not protect every SIP field or decide whether a call should be accepted.

sections.title: Changes from the Earlier Specification
sections.content:
RFC 8224 obsoletes RFC 4474 and states that the earlier mechanism was not believed to have been deployed or implemented in deployed products. This revision replaces the earlier signature format with PASSporT, moves credential information into Identity parameters, and permits multiple Identity headers in one request.

It also narrows which request fields are signed and adds protection for media key fingerprints in SDP. Credential enrollment, acquisition policy, and trust decisions remain outside this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: This version replaces the earlier design with PASSporT and a revised Identity header. It leaves credential enrollment and trust policy to other specifications.
